The View from SomewherePart II · Price levels across countries

Chapter 6

Tastes that move

Web edition. Figure 6.2 is live: it opens on the book’s draw, and its controls simulate new economies of the same design.

Here is an invented loop. Three countries, A, B and C, and a price index computed from each pair’s expenditure data. The index says prices in B run 4.0 percent above prices in A. It says prices in C run 3.0 percent above B. And, computed directly from the data of A and C, it says prices in C run 6.0 percent above A. Go from A to C by way of B and you get 1.04×1.03=1.0712. Go directly and you get 1.06. The two routes differ by a factor of 1.0712/1.06=1.0106, about one percent, and nothing in the data of any one pair is wrong.

Chapter 5 introduces the standard repair. Official statistics takes the three bilateral numbers and replaces them with the closest set that does close, in the least-squares sense, which is what GEKS computes, and it throws the discrepancy away. This chapter is about the discrepancy. If the index is the one that is exact for constant-elasticity demand, and a loop still fails to close, something in the countries must differ. The obvious suspect is taste.

I will tell you where the chapter ends, because it is not where we hoped it would end. The identity that connects the discrepancy to taste is in print, in Redding and Weinstein (2020), written for two dates instead of two countries. The condition under which the discrepancy vanishes is in print too, in Abe and Rao (2019). The memo’s conclusion is that the proposition is theirs. What our cycle added is a numerical check, a warning about the Fisher index, and a way of drawing the whole thing so that you can see which part of a taste difference an index loop can detect and which part it cannot. That last part is worth the chapter.

6.1A loop is a plane and a line

Take the log of a bilateral index and write xjk for the log price level of country k relative to country j. A price index worth the name has xkj=−xjk. Call a set of such numbers transitive if there are country levels ϕ1,ϕ2,ϕ3 with xjk=ϕk−ϕj on every pair. In the language of Part I the xjk are numbers on the edges of a graph, a transitive set is a coboundary, and the loop sum L=x12+x23+x31 is the obstruction. It is zero on every coboundary, and for the triangle it is all there is to the obstruction, because the triangle has one independent loop. (A graph with E edges and N nodes has E−N+1 of them; the complete graph on eight countries in the experiments below has 28−8+1=21.)

A triangle’s edge data live in R3, one coordinate per edge, and the geometry is easy to see (Figure 6.1). The transitive vectors satisfy x12+x23+x31=0, so they fill a plane through the origin. That plane has two free parameters, which are the two independent differences in ϕ; the level of ϕ itself never enters. Its normal direction is (1,1,1). Any edge vector splits uniquely into a point of the plane plus a multiple of the normal, x=g+L3(1,1,1),g=(x12−L3,x23−L3,x31−L3),x=g+L3(1,1,1),g=(x12−L3,x23−L3,x31−L3), and g is the nearest transitive vector. You can check that GEKS gives exactly this. The GEKS parity for the pair (1,2) averages x1m+xm2 over m=1,2,3. The terms for m=1 and m=2 both equal x12, and the term for m=3 is −x31−x23, so the average is (2x12−x23−x31)/3=x12−L/3. On a triangle, GEKS takes the discrepancy and spreads it equally over the three edges.

I want you to keep this picture, because the argument of the chapter happens in it. Whatever economics puts into an index vector, an index loop sees only the height above the plane. Everything that moves the vector within the plane is invisible to it.

6.2CES demand and the logarithmic mean

Consumers in country c choose among goods i=1,…,I with CES preferences, elasticity of substitution σ>1 the same in every country, and a taste shifter bic>0 that may differ by country. Write βic=log⁡bic. With prices pic, expenditure shares are sic=bicpic1−σPc1−σ,Pc1−σ=∑ibicpic1−σ,sic=bicpic1−σPc1−σ,Pc1−σ=∑ibicpic1−σ, and Pc is country c’s own CES price level. In logs, (1)log⁡sic=βic+(1−σ)log⁡pic−(1−σ)log⁡Pc. Two features matter. First, only relative tastes within a country change behavior: multiply every bic in country c by one constant and the shares do not move, because Pc1−σ absorbs the constant. So the level of taste in a country cannot be separated from its price level. Redding and Weinstein (2020) fix this by normalizing the geometric mean of tastes; some normalization is needed or no index is defined. Second, equation (1) says that the share of good i moves with its price, with its taste, and with the country’s overall price level, all through logs, which is what makes the algebra below short.

The Sato–Vartia index weights each good’s log price ratio by a logarithmic mean of its two shares. The logarithmic mean of two positive numbers is L(a,b)=a−blog⁡a−log⁡b,L(a,a)=a,L(a,b)=a−blog⁡a−log⁡b,L(a,a)=a, which lies between a and b. For a pair of countries (j,k) put wijk=L(sij,sik)∑hL(shj,shk),SVjk=∑iwijk(log⁡pik−log⁡pij).wijk=L(sij,sik)∑hL(shj,shk),SVjk=∑iwijk(log⁡pik−log⁡pij). The weights are positive, sum to one and are symmetric in j and k, so SVkj=−SVjk. They also have one property that does all the work. Because L(a,b)(log⁡a−log⁡b)=a−b, (2)∑iwijk(log⁡sik−log⁡sij)=∑i(sik−sij)∑hL(shj,shk)=1−1⋯=0. Weighted by wjk, the log share changes cancel. That is the defining trick of the index, and it is why it is exact when tastes are common: it removes the share changes that equation (1) would otherwise have to carry.

6.3The identity

Proposition. For every pair of countries, SVjk=(log⁡Pk−log⁡Pj)+θjk,θjk=1σ−1∑iwijk(βik−βij).SVjk=(log⁡Pk−log⁡Pj)+θjk,θjk=1σ−1∑iwijk(βik−βij).

Proof. Difference equation (1) across the pair: Δlog⁡si=Δβi+(1−σ)Δlog⁡pi−(1−σ)Δlog⁡P. Multiply by wijk and sum over goods. The left side is zero by (2). The right side is ∑iwiΔβi+(1−σ)SVjk−(1−σ)Δlog⁡P, using that the weights sum to one. Solve for SVjk. ◻

The first term, log⁡Pk−log⁡Pj, is a difference of two country-level numbers. It is a coboundary and contributes nothing to any loop. So the loop sum of the Sato–Vartia index is the loop sum of the taste term: SV12+SV23+SV31=θ12+θ23+θ31. Figure 6.2 shows this for one draw from an economy of the kind used in the experiments, three countries and twenty goods with σ=4, log prices of standard deviation 0.3, and a component of taste specific to country and good, with standard deviation τ=0.8. The draw is one of the typical ones: its loop sum is larger in absolute value than 29 percent of 2,000 draws from the same design, and smaller than the rest. Read each row from left to right. The light bar is the price-level part of the edge, the dark bar starts where the light bar ends and is the taste part, and the dot is where they land, the index itself.

Two things in the picture deserve a remark. On two of the three edges the price-level parts are big, up to 0.22, and the taste parts offset most of them. That is the normalization at work: log⁡Pc contains the tastes in country c, and the taste term takes them out again. If you rescale every taste in a country by a constant, both parts change and their sum, the index, does not. Only the sum is a measurement, and the loop sum of the sum is unaffected.

The second remark is that the loop sum here, −0.0275 in logs, is a discrepancy of about 2.8 log points. The same draw gives loop sums of −0.0109 for the Törnqvist index and −0.0110 for the Fisher index. These are one triangle. The averages over many economies are in Section 6.5, and the ordering of the three indexes there is not the ordering in this draw.

6.4What glues and what does not

The identity is exact, so it can be asked three questions in turn. When is the loop sum zero? What does it measure when it is not? And what can it never see?

Common tastes. If βic=βi for every country, then θjk=0 and SVjk=log⁡Pk−log⁡Pj, an exact coboundary. Fisher’s circularity test is passed exactly, even though the weights wjk still differ from pair to pair, because the shares themselves differ with prices. The experiment confirmed it: at τ=0 the share of the index’s variation that fails to glue was of order 10−27, which is rounding error.

Pair-invariant weights. Suppose the weights did not depend on the pair, wjk=w¯ for all pairs. Then θjk=1σ−1∑iw¯i(βik−βij)=Bk−Bj,Bc=1σ−1∑iw¯iβic,θjk=1σ−1∑iw¯i(βik−βij)=Bk−Bj,Bc=1σ−1∑iw¯iβic, again a coboundary. Differences in taste, however large, leave no trace on any loop; they are absorbed into what looks like a difference in price levels. The experiment built a taste term this way, with weights fixed at the average share, at τ=0.8, and it glued to 10−31. This is the condition in Abe and Rao’s Proposition 2, and I come back to how to read it in the section on the papers.

The loop sum itself. Now let both vary. Write out the loop sum of θ and collect terms by country. Country 1 appears in edge 1→2 with a minus sign and in edge 3→1 with a plus sign, so β1 is multiplied by w31−w12; the same bookkeeping for the other two gives (3)θ12+θ23+θ31=1σ−1∑i[βi1(wi31−wi12)+βi2(wi12−wi23)+βi3(wi23−wi31)]. Each country’s taste vector is paired with the difference between the weights of the two pairs that country belongs to. We checked (3) against the direct computation on 2,000 random triangles; the largest gap was 1.7×10−16. The formula says three things.

  • The weights in each bracket sum to zero over goods, since each wjk sums to one. So adding the same constant to every taste in a country changes nothing, which is the normalization again.

  • If βic=αi for all c (common tastes), the three brackets add to ∑iαi⋅0=0, so the loop closes. More generally, if βic=αi+γc, a good effect plus a country effect, the loop closes too: the γc drop out by the first point and the αi by the second. In 2,000 draws of that kind the largest loop sum was 5.6×10−16. This case is less rich than it looks. A country effect γc multiplies every taste in country c by the same constant, and Section 6.2 showed that shares cannot see that, so an additive taste structure produces exactly the shares of common tastes, and the loop closing is the normalization again (Try it 6.2). So what glues is taste differences that are additive in logs across goods and countries. What does not glue is the interaction, the way one country’s tastes depart from another’s differently for different goods, and only where the weights also differ across pairs.

  • Redding and Weinstein’s condition for the Sato–Vartia bias to vanish is that taste shocks are orthogonal to the weights, as our notes record it. Equation (3) is the same statement in cross-section. If tastes are normalized so that the mean of βic over goods is the same in every country, then ∑iwijkΔβi=∑i(wijk−1I)Δβi: the taste term is I/(σ−1) times a covariance across goods between the weights and the taste difference. The normalization is theirs, applied across countries instead of dates, and we have not seen it written that way.

That is the sense in which the loop residual is a lower bound on taste heterogeneity, and I want to state it with care, because the phrase in the memo is looser than the mathematics. A zero loop sum is compatible with large taste differences: the additive ones, and any others that formula (3) happens to weight to zero. A non-zero loop sum proves that tastes are neither common nor additive. Formula (3) is linear in the taste matrix once the weights are fixed, and the weights are computed from observed shares, so for observed weights the loop sum is ℓ(β) for a known linear map ℓ, and the size of the non-additive part of the taste matrix is at least |ℓ(β)| divided by the norm of ℓ, a norm that contains the factor 1/(σ−1). That is a statement about size, in the units of β, and it needs σ. It is a one-sided instrument: it can detect and it cannot certify. There is a second reason to be careful. The weights themselves depend on tastes through the shares, so the map ℓ is not fixed in any thought experiment that varies β.

In the language of the first book this is the old story of agreement after translation. Parties with different frames can agree completely once you translate between them, and a loop test cannot tell that from parties with the same frame. The memo also cautions against leaning on the analogy, since a taste shifter is a preference parameter and a frame, in the original idea, was about how a person renders what they hold into terms another can use. I leave the analogy there.

6.5Formula error

The Sato–Vartia index is exact for the CES preferences of Section 6.2 when tastes are common. Fisher’s and Törnqvist’s are not; they are the familiar workhorses of Chapter 5, each exact for a different family of preferences, and for CES at this elasticity each is only an approximation. Approximation errors vary from pair to pair, and errors that vary from pair to pair do not telescope. So Fisher and Törnqvist indexes should fail circularity even when tastes are identical, and the experiment says they do.

The design was eight countries, twenty goods, σ=4, log prices with standard deviation 0.3, and taste shifters with a good-specific component common to all countries, of standard deviation 0.5, plus a country-and-good-specific component of standard deviation τ. Two hundred economies per value of τ, from exp2_price_index_circularity.py. Let t be the vector of an index’s 28 pair values, and let r be its component that does not glue, the vector minus its nearest coboundary. The table reports the mean of r⋅r/t⋅t, the share of the index’s squared variation that does not glue, and the root mean square of r.

share not gluing RMS of r
τ SV Törn. Fisher SV Törn. Fisher
0.0 0.0% 3.5% 10.9% 0.000 0.019 0.037
0.1 0.2% 4.0% 12.0% 0.004 0.020 0.037
0.2 0.8% 4.4% 12.2% 0.009 0.023 0.040
0.4 2.7% 6.0% 12.7% 0.018 0.027 0.041
0.8 9.1% 12.9% 18.2% 0.036 0.045 0.055

Three findings, as in the memo. With common tastes the Sato–Vartia index has no obstruction, to machine precision. Its obstruction grows with taste dispersion, close to linearly in root-mean-square terms: the ratio of RMS to τ is 0.0448, 0.0453, 0.0441 and 0.0455 at the four positive values. And Fisher and Törnqvist fail circularity with identical tastes: 10.9 and 3.5 percent of their variation does not glue, purely because neither formula is exact for these preferences.

The third finding is a warning, and it is the one to carry out of this chapter. The memo notes that official parities are built on Fisher indexes. A loop residual in a Fisher-based comparison is then largely formula error, at least at low taste dispersion, and it cannot be read as evidence of taste differences. The decomposition should not be pushed further than the experiment allows. At τ=0 the whole Fisher residual is formula error. At τ>0 the experiment does not split what is formula error from what is taste; the two do not add in any simple way, and the share panel’s denominators differ across the indexes. At τ=0.8 the Fisher residual is 0.055 in RMS against 0.037 with common tastes, and we would not put more of a reading on that than the numbers carry.

The formula error also depends on how elastic demand is. We ran the three-country economy of Figure 6.2 with 3,000 economies per setting (figures/ch06_sigma.py) and report the root mean square of the per-edge residual, which for a triangle is |L|/3, for Sato–Vartia, Törnqvist and Fisher:

τ=0 τ=0.8
σ SV Törn. Fisher SV Törn. Fisher
2 0.000 0.002 0.009 0.024 0.025 0.027
4 0.000 0.013 0.025 0.025 0.030 0.036
8 0.000 0.047 0.056 0.025 0.052 0.059

With identical tastes the approximation error of Fisher and Törnqvist grows steeply with σ, and at σ=8 it exceeds what the Sato–Vartia index shows at τ=0.8. The Sato–Vartia residual hardly moves with σ at all. That is a little surprising, since formula (3) carries a factor 1/(σ−1); the weights must change with σ in a way that offsets it, because larger σ makes shares respond more to prices. We have not worked that out. It is an observation about this design.

Redding and Weinstein report something that looks at first as if it contradicts this. Over time, in their scanner data, the difference between the Sato–Vartia and Fisher indexes has a standard deviation of only about 0.06 percentage points a year. In our cross-country simulation Fisher fails circularity far more than Sato–Vartia. The two are different comparisons, the level of an index across dates against the consistency of its loops across places, and both can hold. A small difference in levels says nothing about whether the approximation errors telescope.

6.6Two knobs

The memo ties the residual to taste dispersion. The identity suggests it also depends on how much prices vary: if every price is the same in every country, every index is zero and so is every loop. The memo’s experiment held price variation fixed at 0.3. For this chapter we wrote a second, seeded script figures/ch06_surface.py with the same design (eight countries, twenty goods, σ=4) and 150 economies per cell, varying both τ from 0 to 1 and the standard deviation of log prices from 0 to 0.6. Figure 6.4 shows the RMS Sato–Vartia residual over the grid.

The surface is zero along both edges, which is the identity at one edge (τ=0: exact index) and trivial at the other (no price variation: nothing to index). In between it is very nearly the product of the two knobs. In the 30 cells where both are positive the ratio of the residual to τ× price dispersion lies between 0.144 and 0.157, with mean 0.151; and 0.15×0.3=0.045 is the slope of the memo’s line. That is a feature of this design, not something we have derived, and we would not extrapolate it beyond twenty goods, eight countries and σ=4. A rough reading, which is a hypothesis and not a result, is that the residual needs two things at once: taste differences that vary by good, so the weights differ in the way equation (3) rewards, and price differences to weight, so that the index has something to carry. A bilinear form is what two such ingredients would give.

6.7What the papers say

What the paper says: Redding and Weinstein (2020), “Measuring aggregate price indices with taste shocks: theory and evidence for CES preferences”

Their problem is the standard one in the economics of price indexes, over time. If consumers have CES preferences and tastes move, what does the Sato–Vartia index measure? They show in their equation (13) that the exact CES index equals the Sato–Vartia index minus a share-weighted sum of log taste changes, which they call the taste-shock bias. The bias vanishes when taste shocks are uncorrelated with the expenditure-share weights, and the paper stresses that chaining does not remove it. They estimate it at about 0.4 percentage points a year in scanner data. They fix the level of taste by holding the geometric mean of tastes constant across common varieties, which is the “level not identified” fact of Section 6.2. They also use the Sato–Vartia assumption of no taste shocks as an overidentifying restriction: under it the elasticity of substitution can be recovered from any weighting, and the estimate they get that way is wildly unstable, with a median of −2.55 and a standard deviation of 196, and they use that instability as a specification test of the no-taste-shocks assumption.

Our proposition is their equation (13) with two countries where they have two dates; the factor 1/(σ−1) comes from how the taste parameter is scaled here. What the paper does not do, in the passages we have: it does not discuss transitivity or circularity, and cross-country comparison appears only in its review of the literature. A search of the whole text found nothing on circularity, but the stored text was extracted from a PDF, so a missed passage is possible. Reading depth: all prose of the main text, pages 503 to 557. The displayed equations and tables did not extract cleanly, so equation (13) is known to us from the prose around it, not from a clean copy of the formula, and the online appendix was not read.

What the paper says: Abe and Rao (2019), “Multilateral Sato–Vartia index for international comparisons of prices and real expenditures”

This is a discussion paper from Hitotsubashi. It starts from the observation that the Sato–Vartia index has not been used for multilateral comparisons because it is not transitive. Their Proposition 2 says it is transitive if and only if its weights do not depend on the pair of countries. They propose four transitive versions, with weights that do not, chosen close to the observed ones, and apply them to 2011 International Comparison Program household-consumption data, 47 countries and 139 basic headings. Their distance Δ1, the root-mean-square gap between a transitive index and the binary Sato–Vartia index, is between 0.046 and 0.048 across the methods, and the six transitive indexes they compute correlate above 0.999 with one another.

This is the paper that states the invariance condition. It treats intransitivity as a defect to be removed and does not relate its size to tastes. Reading depth: main text pages 1 to 7 and the data and weighting appendix; the proofs in the appendix were not read, so Proposition 2 is known to us from its statement. One more thing about that statement, which is our reading and not the paper’s. Under common tastes the weights still vary from pair to pair, because shares vary with prices, and yet the loops close exactly, as the experiment confirmed. So the “only if” cannot be about a particular data set. It must be a statement about the formula over arbitrary data, and a data set generated by CES with common tastes is a special case in which the formula is transitive anyway.

What the paper says: Sato and Vartia, the original index papers

We did not read them. Everything above about the index comes from its description in the two papers just discussed, and the exactness for CES with common tastes, which the experiment confirmed to machine precision, from the identity itself.

What the paper says: Hill (1999); a Statistics Netherlands discussion paper (2017); a 2025 paper on the empirical welfare content of international comparisons (arXiv:2504.16654)

Hill’s proposal is to chain bilateral comparisons along the spanning tree that minimizes the spread between Paasche and Laspeyres indexes. Chaining along a tree makes the result transitive by construction and discards every loop. Like GEKS it lands on a coboundary, though not in general the nearest one, since the tree’s own edges are kept exactly. We read Hill in summary. The Statistics Netherlands paper, of which we read the summary and Section 2, draws the same picture as a “price index digraph” whose cycles should have product one and treats transitivity as a requirement to be met. The 2025 paper, which we have read only in summary, finds that 3 to 5 percent of country pairs fall outside non-homothetic bounds for GEKS parities and proposes taste-corrected values. None of these relates the loop residual to taste dispersion in the sections read, and the last is a different route to the same worry.

What the paper says: Malaney and Weinstein; Nguyen (arXiv:2112.03460)

Malaney and Weinstein recast index numbers as parallel transport in a gauge theory. Nguyen argues that their central corollary is a tautology once translated back into economics and that a conjecture is false as stated. We read only a summary. It is a caution for us: a geometric restatement of index numbers is not a result by being geometric, and this chapter’s pictures have to earn their place the same way.

6.8What we found

Cycle 2 asked whether the part of a bilateral index that fails to glue carries information about tastes. We had in mind the nearest thing standard economics has to different frames.

The experiment. Section 6.5 gave the design and the table. The numerical checks on the same economies were: the proposition’s consequence for loops, that the index and the taste term have the same obstruction, held to 3×10−13 in every draw (the largest gap was 2.97×10−13, at τ=0); GEKS equaled the least-squares gluing part of Fisher indexes to 3.3×10−16; and a taste term built with pair-invariant weights glued to 10−31.

The first verdict. The notebook’s first verdict was one clean identity, numerically confirmed, joining the obstruction to something economists care about, and showing what a loop statistic can and cannot see. Its novelty was marked unverified.

The correction. We then read the two papers that could settle novelty, and the verdict changed. The proposition is Redding and Weinstein’s equation (13), across countries instead of dates. The invariance condition is Abe and Rao’s Proposition 2. Neither paper, in the sections read, puts the two together: Redding and Weinstein do not discuss circularity, and Abe and Rao do not discuss tastes. What remains, in the memo’s words, is a remark, perhaps a short note with data, and not a theorem. The remark has three parts. The circularity residual of the Sato–Vartia index across countries is exactly the non-gluing part of the taste term. It is therefore a lower bound on taste heterogeneity, in the one-sided sense of Section 6.4. And the Fisher-based residual is contaminated by formula error. The memo’s list of survivors calls this a reading of two known results together. That description is right in kind and in size.

The notes on Abe and Rao. The first reading notes on Abe and Rao said that their correlations above 0.999 suggest the circularity residual is small in practice. That was wrong twice over. The correlations are among transitive variants, not between a transitive index and the binary one. And their Δ1, about 0.047 in logs, is larger than the 0.036 our simulation produced at its highest taste dispersion; basic headings are also much coarser than goods, and real data include everything the simulation left out. The notes were corrected the same day. Writing this chapter we noticed that the corrected note may itself be too confident. Δ1 is the gap between a particular transitive index and the binary one. The least-squares residual is the smallest such gap over all transitive indexes that average the same way, so if Δ1 is a root mean square over country pairs, as we read it, the least-squares residual on the same data is no larger than 0.046 and could be much smaller. So 0.047 is better read as a ceiling on the residual than as its value. How Δ1 is averaged is not settled here: its definition, their equation (16) in the main text, is ambiguous as printed. Either way, the residual in real data has not been measured here.

What was not done. The simulation gave every country the same list of goods. In practice countries sell different goods, and a bilateral index is computed on the overlap. That is the structure with different stalks, which the memo then called the part of the framework that is not already index-number theory. Chapter 7 takes it up and finds that it is index-number theory too: Feenstra’s variety adjustment. Sampling error in prices and shares was not modeled, so nothing here says what sample size would detect τ=0.2, where less than one percent of the variation fails to glue. The identity depends on CES with one elasticity; under other preferences the Sato–Vartia residual mixes taste differences with non-homotheticity and misspecification, and the proposition says nothing. The next steps the notebook listed, rerun with partly overlapping goods, add sampling error, and only then look at International Comparison Program data, were not carried out for this cycle.
